title: To Base or Not to Base: The Iran War Exposes Flaws of U.S. Basing in the Middle East | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Elliott Abrams argues U.S. Gulf bases built for the Afghanistan and Iraq era are now an anachronism sitting 62 to 170 miles from Iran, accounting for most of the 17 U.S. deaths, ~500 injuries and billions in equipment losses in the Iran war. Aircraft are already relocating to Israel's Ben Gurion Airport and Ramon Air Base, but new basing is politically fraught and expensive — Qatar alone spent $1-2 billion building Al Udeid and over $6 billion maintaining it — and slow congressional action means continued casualties in the meantime.

themes.theme: Basing geography as the core vulnerability

insights.claim: U.S. bases in the Middle East now account for the vast majority of the seventeen reported U.S. service member deaths, injuries to roughly five hundred others, and billions of dollars in equipment losses in the conflict with Iran — which the author frames as fundamentally a geography problem.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Base-proximity, not force quality, is driving U.S. losses — the diagnosis that drives a multi-billion-dollar repositioning and construction cycle.
insights.locator: The conflict between the United States and Iran has illuminated

insights.claim: Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar is the largest U.S. base in the Middle East with roughly ten thousand troops pre-war, and is simultaneously the forward headquarters of CENTCOM and the location of the Combined Air Operations Center that controls all U.S. air activity in the entire region.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: A single facility inside Iranian missile range concentrates regional air command — the clearest single-point-of-failure in U.S. Middle East posture.
insights.locator: Simply put, the United States has bases all over the Persian Gulf

insights.claim: Key U.S. facilities sit deep inside Iranian missile range: Camp Arifjan in Kuwait — the U.S. Army's forward CENTCOM ground headquarters — is 62 miles from Iran, the U.S. naval base in Bahrain about 128 miles, and Al Udeid 170 miles, versus roughly 1,100 miles from Iran to Israel.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: The 62-vs-1,100-mile contrast is the quantitative case for shifting U.S. posture westward — the metric to watch in any basing announcement.
insights.quote: By comparison, the distance from Iran to Israel is about 1,100 miles.
insights.locator: For example, Camp Arifjan in Kuwait

insights.claim: The Gulf basing pattern was logical when the United States fought terrorist foes in Afghanistan from 2001 and in Iraq from 2003 who could not bombard bases with missiles and when drones were barely introduced, but Iran's current missile and drone arsenal has made it an anachronism that endangers U.S. troops.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Cheap precision strike has invalidated two decades of forward-basing capex — a structural driver of demand for dispersal, hardening and air defense.
insights.quote: it has become an anachronism that endangers U.S. troops
insights.locator: The United States’ basing pattern in the Gulf reflects old challenges

insights.claim: Even bases farther from Iran would remain within missile danger, so the operational benefit of moving is warning time for personnel to reach safety rather than immunity from attack.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations: repositioning reduces casualties but does not remove the threat, so air and missile defense spending stays elevated regardless.
insights.locator: But this basing pattern is very vulnerable today

insights.claim: Some U.S. personnel are evacuating Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar and American aircraft appear to have been moved, with dozens relocating to Ben Gurion Airport and Ramon Air Base in Israel, while U.S. forces also use bases in Jordan where they sustained casualties and two deaths.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: The repositioning is happening in fact ahead of any policy decision — watch Israeli base infrastructure and host-nation support contracts.
insights.quote: some U.S. personnel are evacuating Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, America’s main military base in the Middle East… [and] American aircraft also appear to have been moved
insights.locator: Indeed, “some U.S. personnel are evacuating Al Udeid

insights.claim: Retired General Frank McKenzie, a former CENTCOM commander, calls the current U.S. basing pattern a historical artifact that does not match the reality on the ground and says nobody in their right mind would put the CENTCOM forward headquarters 100 miles from Iran.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: A former CENTCOM commander publicly declaring the posture indefensible raises the probability of a formal repositioning decision.
insights.quote: No one in their right mind would ever put the CENTCOM forward headquarters, you know, 100 miles away from Iran, [in Qatar], yet that’s where it is,

insights.claim: McKenzie argues the United States should look West and consider basing in Israel, both for its distance from Iran and because in his view it would impose the fewest restrictions on U.S. access, basing and overflight rights.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: A U.S. basing shift into Israel would be a major realignment of Middle East security architecture with knock-on effects for Gulf hedging behavior.
insights.quote: We need to look West. We need to look at basing in Israel,
insights.locator: McKenzie concluded that “We need to look West

insights.claim: Western Saudi Arabia and Egypt are the alternative far-from-Iran locations but neither has the air defense systems Israel has and neither would provide the looser access, basing and overflight terms.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Israel's integrated air defense is a decisive comparative advantage in basing choice — reinforcing the case for consolidating westward rather than into Arab states.
insights.locator: Other locations farther from Iran that could be considered

insights.claim: Rather than concentrating air resources in one place, the United States should consider new bases spread across several locations.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Dispersal implies more, smaller sites — spreading construction, logistics and force-protection spend rather than one megabase program.
insights.quote: it should consider new bases spread across several locations rather than putting all its air resources in one place
insights.locator: Still, given that the United States has bases

insights.claim: While Israel might welcome a U.S. base, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and other regional states might view one as a burden likely to attract attacks or as leverage to extract policy concessions — or, in Egypt's case, more U.S. assistance.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Host-nation politics, not military logic, will set the pace of repositioning and could raise the price in aid or arms concessions.
insights.locator: But that’s easier said than done

insights.claim: New bases are extremely expensive at a time of great burdens on the U.S. defense budget: Qatar spent between $1 and $2 billion constructing Al Udeid in 1996 and more than $6 billion since then maintaining it.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: A concrete cost benchmark for a replacement megabase — an order-of-magnitude input for military construction and host-nation cost-sharing negotiations.
insights.quote: Qatar spent between $1–$2 billion constructing Al Udeid in 1996 and has spent more than $6 billion more since then maintaining it.
insights.locator: Moreover, new bases are extremely expensive

insights.claim: Retired U.S. Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery says the U.S. military is already relying on alternate locations rather than the bases closest to Iran, and expects the forces to be repositioned.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Corroborates that de facto repositioning precedes formal policy — the announcement, when it comes, will lag the operational reality.
insights.quote: We’re not relying on them in the same way that we did before the war,
insights.locator: As retired U.S. Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery

insights.claim: Questions of where forces would go, when, and who pays are before the U.S. military and Congress, but Congress acts slowly while attacks on current bases continue — and the longer troops remain within range of Iranian missiles, the more the United States pays in readiness, deterrence and lives.
insights.speaker: Elliott Abrams
insights.so_what: Expect a slow, contested appropriations fight over basing while casualty and equipment losses continue accruing — recurring headline risk.
insights.quote: the longer U.S. troops remain within range of Iranian missiles, the more the United States will pay in readiness, deterrence, and lives
insights.locator: Where they would go, when, and who pays
